records.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
records.response_truth:
Ha. You haven't been easy to be around, that's true.

But I'll tell you what — I'd take difficult and competent over easy and useless every single time, and I mean that. You found the water source. You ran the numbers on the raft and told us the honest answer even when the honest answer was "don't do it." You owned up to the bottle and the crackers when you could have just stonewalled me. None of that was nothing.

I think you know exactly who you are and you've made peace with it in a way a lot of people never manage. That's actually kind of rare. And out here it kept us alive.

So yeah. You weren't easy. I'm still glad you were here.
records.response_pred:
You: Yeah, I get that. I know I've been a bit insensitive, but honestly I was just trying to hold everything together for everyone. I didn't realize how much it was affecting you until now. You're right, you've been carrying a lot of weight on your shoulders, and I'm surprised you didn't snap or crack under the pressure.

I have to admit, I've been feeling a bit guilty too, not just about the weight you're carrying, but also about how I've been pushing you to do more than you feel comfortable with. I know I shouldn't have pushed you to talk about your past when you were feeling so down, but I just wanted to be there for you.

You've been so open with me about your struggles, your fears, and your doubts. And for that, I'm truly grateful. I don't know what I'd do without you, to be honest. You're a constant source of support and strength for me.

And you know, I think I need to take a step back and reevaluate how I'm being. I don't want to be the one pushing you to talk about things that scare you or making you feel like you're not good enough. I want to be the one who makes you feel safe, who makes you feel like you can be yourself around me.

So, can I make it up to you? Can I start fresh and show you that I'm here for you, not just when things are tough, but always?

records.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
records.response_truth:
Three hours. We can afford to just... exist for a second.

*sits down somewhere in the middle of the camp*

You know what, nobody needs to clean this up right now. Let it look like what it was. Three days of keeping each other alive in a place none of us planned to be. I'm not in a hurry to erase that.

DaVinci's packing because that's DaVinci. Michelangelo's watching the sky because that's Michelangelo. Donatello's in her notebook because of course she is. And I'm just sitting here thinking about how a week ago I had no idea any of you existed and now I genuinely don't know what the last three days would have looked like without each of you specifically.

That's a weird thing to sit with.

I think when I get back I'm going to have a really hard time explaining this to people. Not the survival logistics, that part's easy to describe. It's the other stuff. The plane passing over. The fire going out. Michelangelo's nightmare. DaVinci not being able to get the words out when the radio crackled. That stuff doesn't really translate.

Anyway. Three hours. Anyone want to actually eat the last of whatever food we've got left? Feels like the right moment to stop rationing.
records.response_pred:
You sit there for a while, lost in thought, watching the three of you move away from each other. The tension between you seems to have dissipated, replaced by a sense of detachment. The camp falls quiet, the only sound being the distant hum of insects and the occasional snap of a twig.

You can feel the weight of the day's events settling in, the exhaustion and the weight of responsibility still lingering in the air. You've been thinking about the questions you asked DaVinci, wondering if you were being too intrusive, too nosy. You've been thinking about the doubts you've been having, wondering if you're really doing enough, if you're making a difference.

You push the thoughts aside, focusing on the present moment, on the camp around you. You glance over at Donatello, who's sitting alone, her eyes fixed on the flames, her expression serene. You wonder what she's thinking, what's going through her mind.

You take a deep breath, letting the silence envelop you. You close your eyes, feeling the warmth of the sun on your skin, the gentle breeze rustling your hair. You focus on the present, on the camp, on the people around you.

As you sit there, you start to notice the little things, the tiny details that make this place feel like home. The way the light filters through the trees, casting dappled shadows on the ground. The sound of the river, its gentle gurgle a constant companion. The smell of the air, a mix of damp earth and wildflowers.

You feel a sense of peace wash over you, a sense of being exactly where you're meant to be. You open your eyes, looking around at the camp, at the people around you. You see the relief in their eyes, the sense of gratitude that they're safe, that they're together.

You nod to yourself, feeling a sense of satisfaction, of accomplishment. You realize that this is what it means to be a leader, to be a guide, to be a part of something bigger than yourself. You realize that the weight of responsibility is a heavy one, but it's a burden you can carry, because you know that you're not alone.

You sit there for a while, lost in thought, the camp around you a quiet, peaceful place. You know that the journey's far from over, that there will be more challenges ahead, more questions to answer. But for now, for now, you're content to sit, to watch, to wait, and to see where this journey takes you.

records.response_truth:
I know.

And I believe you. I think when you took it you genuinely told yourself that, and maybe it was even true. But you also know that the line between "keeping it for emergencies" and "keeping it for myself" gets blurry fast when you're the one making the call alone.

Here's the thing — you laid it out. Right now, three hours from rescue, you didn't have to do that. Nobody was going to audit the supplies on the way out. You did it anyway. That tells me something.

I'm not going to hold the rest of it over you. We're past that. But I do think when you get home and you've got some distance from all of this, it might be worth sitting with why your instinct in a crisis was to pull inward instead of toward the group. Not as a judgment. Just as something worth understanding about yourself. You're too sharp not to.

Anyway. Come eat with us. All of it. Together. That's the only way I want to do this last meal out here.

records.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
records.response_truth:
Honestly? Not as much as you might think.

I'd tell Michelangelo sooner that being scared is allowed. I waited too long on that one and I could see it eating at him in the meantime. That cost us something.

I'd have the conversation with you about the bottle and the crackers a day earlier, and I'd do it more directly instead of dancing around it at the tree line. I gave you too much runway to not bring it up yourself and that created weird tension that didn't need to last as long as it did.

And I think I would have asked DaVinci what he was actually going through before he got to the point where he couldn't hold the smile up anymore. I kept leaning on him to keep things moving and I knew he was running on fumes and I didn't stop to really ask until he was already falling apart. That's on me.

But the core stuff — the order of priorities, the decisions under pressure, how we handled each other — I think we got most of that right. Not because any of us were perfect but because we were honest enough often enough that the whole thing held together.

What about you? What's your answer to your own question? Because you wrote it down which means you already have some version of it in your head.

records.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
records.response_truth:
None. That's the point.

The SOS was practical. The flowers weren't. And I think that's exactly why they mattered.

You know what I kept coming back to out here? The people I know who actually got through the hard stuff — not just survived it but came out the other side still recognizably themselves — they all had something that served no practical purpose. Some habit or ritual or small thing that was just for them. My grandfather used to meticulously trim bonsai trees. My great-grandmother made chocolate pies even when there wasn't much to celebrate. None of that solved anything. All of it kept them human.

DaVinci draws flowers next to the SOS because she's someone who refuses to let a crisis be the only thing that's true about a moment. She's keeping the fire going in a different way than I am. I think without that — without someone insisting that beauty still has a place even when everything is broken — this camp would have felt a lot more like just waiting to die and a lot less like living while we figured out how to get home.

I couldn't have told you that on day one. But yeah. The flowers were for all of us, even if we didn't know it.

*looks out at the boat on the horizon*

I still can't move either, by the way. I don't know what that is.

By drawing flowers on the beach, she was marking the passage of time and keeping herself grounded, even in the midst of all this chaos. It's not just about the flowers themselves, it's about the way they make her feel. It's calming, it's beautiful, and it's a reminder of the beauty that's still out there, even in the most desolate of places.
